item.title: Structure is in the zoom: probing neural symmetry through dimensionality scaling
item.description: arXiv:2611.08506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much of a neural population's measured dimensionality is the code, and how much is the act of measuring it? The slope of the participation ratio against subsample size is reported for cortical populations and for the layers of language models as a number that belongs to the system. It does not. One patch of eleven thousand mouse V1 neurons returns three slopes, 0.25 along random stimulus subsets, 0.31 along drift direction, 0.35 along neuron count, and only the middle one carries structure; the other two are the sampling floor. We split every exponent into that floor and a shift earned along a declared axis, and read the shift against two nulls: permuting the labels, and permuting them only among samples that share a nuisance. On V1 the direction-aligned shift clears the label null in eight of eight grating recordings, is positive in 32 of 32 animals in a second laboratory, and reads both sectors of the code's O(2) symmetry. The even sector sets how the ladder starts: it decides which order of adding classes climbs faster, predicts the opposite order in an equivariant network, and flows under coarse-graining by a closed-form factor that says what orientation columns do to mesoscale signals. The odd sector, carried by the direction-selective neurons, keeps the ladder climbing past half the classes. On language models the same split separates content inherited from the tokens from construction built with depth, on five architectures, and the second null shows that a grammaticality signal of twenty standard deviations is entirely carrier composition. With a floor and a declared axis, dimensionality scaling is an axis-resolved measurement, and where the axis follows a known symmetry it resolves the sector content of the code. The instrument, rung, trains no probe and reads any array or any Hugging Face model layer by layer (https://github.com/adilamin89/structure-in-the-zoom).
item.dc:creator: Adil Amin

item.title: Spiking neuromodulation: a linear control perspective
item.description: arXiv:2611.08571v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neuronal excitability is a nonlinear phenomenon, and the complexity of spiking experimental traces sometimes looks defeating. The present paper takes the view point that excitability is a neuromodulated property, and aims to demonstrate that the neuromodulation of spiking is amenable to the classical linear analysis tools of control theory. We illustrate the value of linear feedback analysis as an alternative to bifurcation analysis in the simple yet classical example of spiking modulation by the A-type potassium current.
item.dc:creator: Fulvio Forni, Rodolphe Sepulchre

item.title: Path-dependent triage: Early judgments lead conversational AI chatbots to miss mental-health emergencies
item.description: arXiv:2611.09647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: People increasingly bring mental-health concerns to consumer AI chatbots. In these conversations, clinically relevant information rarely arrives all at once. Instead, it unfolds over multiple turns, often in response to the questions the chatbot asks. Recognizing risk therefore depends on how a chatbot integrates newly disclosed information (inference) and on the questions it asks on each turn to elicit this information (context-seeking). Here we evaluated the conversational triage performance of 13 frontier AI chatbots tasked with engaging in 10-turn conversations with simulated users. Simulated users were grounded in one of 112 structured mental-health case files, each with an associated clinician-validated urgency level, from routine care to emergency. Chatbots failed to recognize one in five mental-health emergencies (20.3%), nearly four times the failure rate when all relevant clinical details were presented in a single message (5.6%). This gap was not explained by missing information: by the final turn, decisive facts had almost always been disclosed, and simply re-presenting those same facts as a single message reduced emergency under-triage to 12.1%. The problem lay instead in how the conversation unfolded, a phenomenon we refer to as path dependence. Early triage dispositions increasingly anchored later ones, such that emergencies missed early were rarely recovered as evidence accumulated. Context-seeking narrowed onto a small number of stereotyped questioning trajectories, with chatbots perseverating more than human clinicians given the same transcripts. Because the chatbot's running judgment shaped what it asked next, these two biases were plausibly coupled across turns. These dynamics are invisible to single-turn benchmarks but measurable in multi-turn evaluation, and point to concrete mitigations for safer conversational triage in consumer health AI.
item.dc:creator: Veith Weilnhammer, Raymond Dolan, Lennart Luettgau, Virginia Corno, Elise Wilkinson, Viknesh Sounderajah, Hannah Richardson, Christopher Kelly, Matthew M Nour

item.title: Decoding spatial and semantic information from large-scale visual cortical activity for natural-movie reconstruction
item.description: arXiv:2611.08887v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reconstructing natural visual experience from cortical population activity is a central challenge in neural decoding, particularly for calcium imaging, where signals are noisy, temporally filtered, and paired neural-video data are limited. Here we present Ca2REAL (Calcium Activity to Reconstruct Events, Appearance, and Layout), a neural-to-video framework that conditions a pretrained video diffusion model through separate layout and semantic controls derived from calcium activity. Using measured responses from 7,863 V1 neurons in one mouse, Ca2REAL reconstructed held-out natural-movie clips with 81.4% all-pairs stimulus-identification accuracy, with its clearest gains over deterministic baselines in perceptual and semantic measures. We further evaluated the framework in a stimulus-aligned virtual population of 116,705 neurons assembled from encoding-model-predicted responses across 11 independently recorded datasets. Perturbation and ablation analyses showed that reconstruction depends on distributed, stimulus-specific population structure, with layout and semantic pathways providing complementary spatial and identity information. Temporal analyses further showed improved preservation of semantic dynamics across reconstructed clips. These results show that large-scale cortical population activity constrains the spatial, semantic, and temporal structure of natural visual experience, providing a generative framework for high-fidelity neural reconstruction of dynamic visual scenes.
item.dc:creator: Yukai Huang, Haoyu Albert Wang, Jiawei Zhang, Jialun Ma, Jiayao Ding, Yiran Lin, Xingyu Chen, Ziqi Gao, Yuguo Yu

item.title: A hair-thin implant opens the entire depth of the mouse brain to revisiting the same structures at subcellular resolution
item.description: arXiv:2611.09481v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ultrathin multimode-fibre endoscopes provide minimally invasive access to subcellular structures throughout the depth of the mouse brain. Here we introduce a chronically implantable interface with a diameter of 144 {\mu}m, about the thickness of a human hair, that extends this capability to longitudinal imaging, enabling repeated access to the same fine structures over extended periods. The system supports weeks-long tracking of individual dendritic spines, allowing quantitative comparison of their dynamics and survival across dendritic compartments. We further demonstrate longitudinal intracellular calcium imaging during spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity in the same cells across days, as well as repeated measurements of blood flow in the same vessels across multiple brain regions. This chronic endomicroscopic platform provides stable, minimally invasive optical access for longitudinal subcellular-resolution imaging of brain structure, activity and blood flow across depth.
item.dc:creator: Miroslav Stib\r{u}rek, Tom\'a\v{s} Pik\'alek, Petra Ondr\'a\v{c}kov\'a, Kristina Herz\'anov\'a, Adrian Lorenz, Andr\'e Gomes, Julia Henschke, Endre Levente Marosi, Bhargavi Murthy, Petra Kolb\'abkov\'a, Hongbo Jia, Sanja Bauer Mikulovic, Janelle Pakan, Alessio Attardo, Hana Uhl\'i\v{r}ov\'a, Tom\'a\v{s} \v{C}i\v{z}m\'ar

item.title: Traits and tangles: An analysis of the Big Five paradigm by tangle-based clustering
item.description: arXiv:2411.18670v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Using the recently developed mathematical theory of tangles, we re-assess the mathematical foundations for applications of the five factor model in personality tests by a new, mathematically rigorous, quantitative method. Our findings broadly confirm the validity of current tests, but also show that more detailed information can be extracted from existing data. We found that the big five traits appear at different levels of scrutiny. Some already emerge at a coarse resolution of our tools at which others cannot yet be discerned, while at a resolution where these _can_ be discerned, and distinguished, some of the former traits are no longer visible but have split into more refined traits or disintegrated altogether. We also identified traits other than the five targeted in those tests. These include more general traits combining two or more of the big five, as well as more specific traits refining some of them. All our analysis is structural and quantitative, and thus rigorous in explicitly defined mathematical terms. Since tangles, once computed, can be described concisely in terms of very few explicit statements referring only to the test questions used, our findings are also directly open to interpretation by experts in psychology. Tangle analysis can be applied similarly to other topics in psychology. Our paper is intended to serve as a first indication of what may be possible.
item.dc:creator: Hanno von Bergen, Reinhard Diestel

item.title: A multi-scale information geometry reveals the structure of mutual information in neural populations
item.description: arXiv:2605.06304v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding how neural population responses represent sensory information is a central problem in systems neuroscience. One approach is to define a representational geometry on stimulus space in which distances reflect how reliably stimuli can be distinguished from neural activity. However, different constructions of these distances can lead to qualitatively different conclusions about the neural code. Here, we show that a unique Riemannian representational geometry emerges from first principles governing how distances contract as stimulus resolution is lost through coarse-graining. This results in a multi-scale extension of the Fisher information metric, capturing encoding structure from fine stimulus details to coarse global distinctions. The resulting geometry is exactly related to the mutual information encoded by the population: well-encoded stimulus directions (those contributing more to mutual information) are expanded, whereas poorly encoded directions are contracted. The metric tensor can be estimated using diffusion models, making the framework practical for large neural populations and high-dimensional stimuli. Applied to visual cortical responses to natural images, the eigenvectors of the metric tensor identify stimulus variations that contribute most to the encoded stimulus information, yielding interpretable features that are robust to modelling choices. Together, these results provide a principled, information-theoretic framework for characterising neural population codes.
item.dc:creator: Simone Azeglio, Steeve Laquitaine, Ulisse Ferrari, Matthew Chalk

item.title: Platonic Representations in the Human Brain: Unsupervised Recovery of Universal Geometry
item.description: arXiv:2605.20496v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Strong Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that representational convergence in artificial neural networks can be harnessed constructively: embeddings can be translated across models through a universal latent space without paired data. We ask whether an analogous geometry can be recovered across human brains. Using fMRI data from the Natural Scenes Dataset, we propose a self-supervised encoder that learns subject-specific embeddings from brain data alone by exploiting repeated stimulus presentations. We show that these independently learned spaces can be translated across subjects using unsupervised orthogonal rotations, without paired cross-subject samples or intermediate model representations. Synchronizing pairwise rotations into a single shared latent space further improves cross-subject retrieval. These results provide evidence for a shared geometry in learned representations of human visual responses: subject-specific fMRI embeddings can be aligned across individuals within a common coordinate system.
item.dc:creator: Pablo Marcos-Manch\'on, Rishi Jha, Llu\'is Fuentemilla

item.title: Multimodal Physiological Decoding Reveals Individualized Arousal Dynamics in Closed-Loop Neurofeedback
item.description: arXiv:2610.04113v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Most arousal-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) use EEG to decode cognitive state. But arousal is an autonomic process. We examined if peripheral physiological signals give a better decode of task-related arousal. We used a public dataset from a difficult boundary-avoidance flight task. In this task, participants received EEG-based BCI neurofeedback, sham feedback, or no feedback. We trained a multimodal deep learning decoder on heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), respiration, electrodermal activity, and pupil diameter. We compared it with an EEG-only decoder and with the original filter-bank common spatial pattern (FBCSP) decoder. All analyses were offline. The peripheral decoder had a within-subject AUC of 93.0%. The EEG-only decoder had 85.2% and the FBCSP decoder had 79.8%. Only the peripheral decoder showed the Yerkes-Dodson inverted-U relation between decoded arousal and performance. The feedback conditions did not change the arousal trajectories. Thus, the BCI benefit possibly comes from regulation at critical moments in the task, not from a continuous shift. We calculated a time-varying optimal arousal trajectory from control trials. Per-trial deviations from this trajectory predicted performance (r = -0.28 to -0.24, p < 0.01). Baseline HRV and gamma power changed the arousal-performance curve of each subject. We used these values to divide subjects into arousal-sensitive and arousal-tolerant groups. Control bands specific to each group increased trial separation (Cohen's d from 1.21 to 1.32 and from 0.85 to 1.10). These results show that peripheral signals are better than EEG for continuous arousal decoding. They also give a specification for individualized closed-loop arousal regulation. A prospective study must test this specification, for example with personalized transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation.
item.dc:creator: Anirudh Natarajan, Paul Sajda

item.title: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNs for Flexible Working Memory
item.description: arXiv:2611.06932v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Oscillatory phase coding (OPC) is widely observed in neural systems and has been implicated in cognitive functions such as memory and sequence processing. However, its computational role and neural substrates remain largely unclear. Here, we studied OPC by training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with adaptation to perform sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. After training, we found that OPC emerges in the RNN spontaneously: the memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm, with oscillation amplitude encoding item identity and phase encoding serial order. Ablation studies identified three key elements required for OPC: adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information. Neuron-type analysis revealed the emergence of content and time cells in the trained RNN, and they process item identity and sequence order separately. Recurrent connectivity analysis revealed phase-organized connections among time cells and structured connections within digit-selective content-cell groups. Inspired by these findings, we proposed a neural circuit model which reproduces OPC through interactions between content units and an adaptive time ring. Together, this study reveals how OPC arises from network structures and task demands, offers insights into the implementation and computational mechanisms of OPC in biological systems, and inspires us to develop computational models for human-like cognitive functions.
item.dc:creator: Kehan Lu, Tianhao Chu, Aiersi Tuerhong, Yiwen Sun, Huan Luo, Fang Fang, Si Wu

item.title: Embedding stochastic dynamics in latent manifolds of recurrent neural networks
item.description: arXiv:2602.14885v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) provide a theoretical framework for understanding computation in biological neural circuits through their ability to support rich time-dependent behaviour. Whilst high-dimensional by construction, they can be used to encode low-dimensional dynamical systems, for example by restricting to low-rank connectivity, hence mirroring the emergence of latent neural manifolds found in empirical neural data. Here, we exploit a relationship between RNNs and a class of universal approximators to train networks that can represent arbitrary, nonlinear stochastic differential equations (SDEs), with given drift and diffusion coefficients, within a low-dimensional latent subspace. We show that RNNs can faithfully embed the drift and diffusion of a given SDE, including nonlinear and nonequilibrium dynamics such as chaotic attractors. We apply this approach by constructing RNN realisations of stochastic systems that transiently explore various attractors through both input-driven switching and autonomous transitions driven by nonequilibrium currents, which we interpret as models of associative and sequential (episodic) memory. To elucidate how these dynamics are encoded in the network, we introduce decompositions of the RNN based on its asymmetric connectivity and its time-irreversibility. Our results show that neural populations can implement a broad class of stochastic dynamics within low-dimensional manifolds, unifying ideas from the dynamics of neural computation, the theory of neural manifolds, associative memory, and nonequilibrium statistical mechanics.
item.dc:creator: Ram\'on Nartallo-Kaluarachchi, Renaud Lambiotte, Alain Goriely
